newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DAX dragged down by Siemens, dollar.
newsitem.headline: German DAX dragged down by Siemens, dollar.

text.p: The German DAX index ended floor dealings on Thursday lower, dragged down by a sharp fall in the shares of German electronic firm Siemens, which had already tumbled in Wednesday's post-bourse electronic trade.
A fall in the dollar of one pfennig to under 1.51 marks, bad for German exporters, also pressured the market and overshadowed an overnight record close on Wall Street.
The DAX index closed floor trade down 15.97 points, or 0.59 percent, at 2,713.22, off the day's low of 2,703.96. Dealers said the index was supported above the 2,700 point level.

Shares pared some of their losses in post-bourse IBIS electronic dealings, after Wall Street opened firmer and the dollar and German Bunds recovered some ground. The IBIS DAX ended down 11.03 points or 0.4 percent at 2,724.25 points.

Siemens, the fifth-heaviest weighted stock among the 30 leading shares which make up the DAX index, had forecast a flat output for the 1996/97 financial year on Wednesday after the close of floor dealings.

The stock dropped to a new year low of 72.90 marks, then recovered slightly to end bourse dealings down 6.93, or 8.6 percent, at 73.27 marks. In IBIS trade the stock recovered somewhat to end up 95 pfennigs at 73.75 marks.

Dealers said they said they expected the German share market to consolidate after it made strides on Wednesday following the results of the U.S. election. "A bit of a rest would be completely healthy," said one trader.
Meanwhile Daimler ended the bourse slightly up, rising 16 pfennigs to 92.85 marks, after releasing nine month sales which were mainly in line with expectations.

In IBIS dealings Daimler slipped 40 pfennigs to 93.30 marks. The industrial giant reported first nine month sales of 75.9 billion marks, up from 72.8 billion a year earlier, a figure one dealer said was "not bad."
Dealers said Daimler, in line with the rest of the German car sector, was suffering from the weaker dollar.
